# Ānāpānassati Sutta (MN 118 (PTS MN iii 78))

**ID:** MN 118 (PTS MN iii 78)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Ānāpānassati Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Mindfulness of Breathing
**PTS:** MN iii 78
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ānāpānassati Sutta* (MN 118; PTS MN iii 78), also known as the *Ānāpānasati Sutta*, is a major exposition on the practice of meditation in the *Majjhimanikāya* [Stanley et al. 2018]. The discourse opens with the Buddha seated among a distinguished assembly of mendicants and arahants on the Uposatha night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, expressing deep satisfaction with their spiritual progress [Karma Sonam Palmo; Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2019]. He then expounds mindfulness of breathing in sixteen sequential steps organized into four tetrads, showing how its cultivation progressively fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which in turn fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), leading ultimately to true knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti*) [Chakma 2015; Stanley et al. 2018; Wen 2011]. The first tetrad, which focuses on the in- and out-breaths as a "body among bodies" (*kāyesu kāyaññatarā*), is directly aligned with the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) and provides a foundation for both meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and insight (*vipassanā*) [Chakma 2015; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2019].

Together with the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (DN 22), MN 118 stands as one of the central canonical reference texts for traditional meditation theory and modern mindfulness practice [McMahan 2008]. Its systematic methodology is extensively treated in later Theravāda exegetical and canonical works such as the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Ānāpānassatikathā*) and the *Visuddhimagga* [Chakma 2015].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: SA 815 布薩; SHT Sutta 84
- Passage-level parallels: SN 54.1 Ekadhammasutta; MN 62 (PTS MN i 420) Mahārāhulovāda Sutta; Bu-Vb Pj3 Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pārājika 3; SA 803 一明
- Resembling parallels: Arv 20 Ṣoḍaśākārā Ānāpāna-Smṛtiḥ; SĀ 810-812; sn54.13-16; SA3 15 一明

**Sources**

- [Chakma 2015] Nirupam Chakma (Ratna Jyoti), Buddhist Meditation: Theory and Practice in the Pali Canon (2015) — Exposition of the sixteen modes of breathing, the first tetrad, and its development through jhāna to vipassanā
- [Stanley et al. 2018] Steven Stanley, Ronald E. Purser, and Nirbhay N. Singh, Handbook of Ethical Foundations of Mindfulness (2018) — Account of the narrative opening with the Saṅgha and the causal chain from ānāpānasati to satipaṭṭhāna, enlightenment factors, and deliverance
- [Karma Sonam Palmo] Karma Sonam Palmo, The Possibility of Female Buddhas in Exoteric Buddhism — Quotation of the opening passage praising the perfected monks in the community
- [Anālayo 2019] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfulness of Breathing: A Practice Guide and Translations (2019) — Analysis of the introductory setting and the alignment of the first tetrad with kāyānupassanā
- [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Discussion of ānāpānasati fulfilling all four satipaṭṭhānas and functioning as a vehicle for both jhāna and insight
- [Wen 2011] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — Analysis of the sixteen steps of ānāpānasati fulfilling the four satipaṭṭhānas
- [McMahan 2008] David L. McMahan, The Making of Buddhist Modernism (2008) — Status of MN 118 alongside DN 22 as foundational texts in the modern mindfulness movement
